intro: Pause for a moment at Nevali Çori, a mound in Şanlıurfa province from the 9th millennium BC. This pre-pottery Neolithic settlement once stood on the Euphrates; today it is flooded by the Atatürk Dam reservoir. It is famous for its cult building and its stone head sculptures.
history: The site was rescued between 1983 and 1991 by a University of Heidelberg team led by Harald Hauptmann. The settlement, dated c. 8400–8100 BC, gave up two remarkable discoveries: a 'cult building' with T-shaped pillars like those of Göbekli Tepe, and the world's oldest domesticated einkorn wheat.
structure-1: Picture first the cult building. This was no ordinary house: it was a purpose-built structure, reserved for religious rituals.
structure-3: Now picture the rectangular houses: the dwellings of the Neolithic settlement, rectangular and tightly clustered together.
structure-4: And then the stone head statues. These are carved human heads, and some of them were portable, made to be carried.
structure-5: Finally, the open area with ovens: an open work area where the ovens were used for communal cooking. Imagine the smoke and the shared meals.
highlights: As you explore, don't miss the T-shaped pillars, the true signature of this place.
facts: Did you know? The salvaged stone heads and the stele known as the 'Nevali Çori Stela' are displayed today in the Şanlıurfa Museum. The site itself lies beneath the Atatürk dam. Its T-shaped pillars were the first sign that such a world existed, years before Göbekli Tepe was dug. And its limestone figures of humans and birds are among the oldest monumental sculpture known.
outro: This brings our journey to Nevali Çori to an end. Please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water. The settlement now rests beneath the water, but its story travels on with you. Enjoy your visit.
